summary: A proposal to improve the early ARPANET flow-control commands "give back" and "return". The author suggests that a give back always be answered by a return and that no further give backs be sent until that reply arrives. The goal is to keep the sender's and receiver's buffer counts from drifting out of step.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 210 proposes changes to the give-back and return flow-control commands. The changes make buffer amounts clearer and require hosts to wait for a reply before sending another give-back.

questions: what did give back and return mean
how did rfc 210 propose to prevent race conditions
why remove fractions from give back commands
subtitle: A proposal to make host buffer allocation updates easier to synchronize.

tldr.problem: The existing give-back and return commands could leave hosts with different views of how much buffer space was allocated.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal makes return report the remaining allocation, requires a return reply before another give-back, and replaces fractional decrements with absolute amounts.
tldr.outcome: The author argues these rules would reduce race conditions and simplify command processing.

today: RFC 210 is a flow-control proposal published in August 1971. The unit metadata lists its status as Unknown.

sections.title: Allocation Information Can Drift
sections.content: The current give-back and return scheme could leave the two hosts out of synchronization. The author argues that a return should report how much space the sender has left after applying a give-back, so the receiving host can learn what allocation the sender believes it has.
sections.plainLanguage: Each host needs to know how much buffer space the other host believes is available. The existing return command did not clearly provide that remaining amount.

sections.title: Sequence Give-Back and Return
sections.content:
Every give-back should receive a return reply, and the receiver should not send another give-back until it receives that return. The sender should also wait until it is no longer awaiting a data RFNM on the relevant link before sending a return.

The author describes the return as effectively a reply to the give-back, and suggests it might be better named accordingly.
sections.plainLanguage: After one host gives back buffer space, the other must reply before another give-back can be sent. This prevents overlapping updates from confusing the allocation count.

sections.title: Use Absolute Decrements
sections.content:
The current give-back command uses fractions and a format unlike allocate and return. The proposal removes fractions and uses absolute decrements in a format like allocate. Allocations cannot be reduced below zero.

If the receiving host estimates the decrement incorrectly, the return reply supplies corrective information.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal uses whole amounts instead of fractions. A return reply can correct the count if the first estimate was wrong.
